sections.title: Two or More Faulty Clocks – Relative Drift Concept
sections.content:
When two clocks gain or lose time at different rates, the key idea is Relative Gain/Loss.

Case 1: Clock A gains 2 minutes/hour, Clock B loses 3 minutes/hour.
Relative difference = 2 + 3 = 5 minutes/hour

4–6 Step Method (Same Time Again):
1. Find the relative drift.
2. One full cycle on a 12-hour dial = 720 minutes.
3. When the relative difference reaches 720 minutes, both clocks will again show the same time.
4. Time = 720 ÷ 5 = 144 hours.
5. 144 hours = 6 days.
6. This is the time when both clocks will again display the same time.

Same Correct Time Again:
1. Clock A's 12-hour error cycle = 720 ÷ 2 = 360 hours
2. Clock B's cycle = 720 ÷ 3 = 240 hours
3. LCM(360,240) = 720 hours
4. After 720 hours both clocks will again show the correct time.

sections.title: Deep Understanding of the 400-Year Gregorian Cycle
sections.content:
In 400 years:
Normal years = 303
Leap years = 97

Total odd days = (303×1 + 97×2) = 303 + 194 = 497
497 ÷ 7 = 71 weeks (remainder 0)

Conclusion: After 400 years the calendar repeats completely.

Last day pattern of century years:
A century year is a leap year only if divisible by 400.
Therefore odd days in:
100 years = 5
200 years = 3
300 years = 1
400 years = 0

Because of this pattern, a century year cannot end on Tuesday, Thursday, or Saturday (cycle of 0,5,3,1 odd days).

sections.title: Abstract Calendar – 8-Day Week
sections.content:
If a week has 8 days
Month = 35 days
Year = 10 months

1 year = 350 days

Question: What will be the 200th day of the 4th year?

Step 1: First 3 years = 3×350 = 1050 days
Step 2: Total days = 1050 + 200 = 1250
Step 3: 1250 ÷ 8 = 156 remainder 2
Step 4: If Day 1 = Monday, remainder 2 → Tuesday

Conclusion: The 200th day will be Tuesday.

sections.title: Faulty Clock + Time Speed Distance Integration
sections.content:
A train travels at 60 km/h and reaches in 5 hours.
The clock becomes 10% slower every hour (geometric slowdown).

Step 1: Actual time = 5 hours
Step 2: Clock shows 60 minutes in the first hour, 54 in the second, 48.6 in the third, etc. (10% less each hour)
Step 3: Use GP sum formula = a(1−r^n)/(1−r)

4–6 Step Method:
1. a = 60, r = 0.9
2. n = 5
3. Total shown time = 60(1−0.9^5)/(0.1)
4. 0.9^5 ≈ 0.59049
5. Sum ≈ 60(1−0.59049)/0.1
6. ≈ 60×0.40951/0.1 ≈ 245.7 minutes

So the clock will show about 4 hours 6 minutes while the actual time passed is 5 hours.

sections.title: Zero-Error Baseline Concept
sections.content:
In complex problems, first set a baseline:
1. When was the clock correct?
2. Keep actual time calculation separate.
3. Track error accumulation separately.
4. Combine both at the end.

Use LCM/HCF for cycle matching.
Relative difference logic is the most important concept.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content:
Relative Drift = Sum/Difference of rates
Same display time → 720 ÷ relative drift
Same correct time → LCM of individual cycles
Calendar repeats after 400 years
In abstract calendar → Total days ÷ days in a week
For geometric faulty clock → Use GP sum

advanced_practice_examples.question: Clock A gains 4 min/hr, Clock B gains 6 min/hr. When will both show the same time?
advanced_practice_examples.solution_steps:
Step 1: Relative gain = 2 min/hr
Step 2: 720 ÷ 2 = 360 hours
Step 3: After 15 days both will show the same time.

advanced_practice_examples.question: Why does the day of 1 January repeat after a 400-year cycle?
advanced_practice_examples.solution_steps:
Step 1: 303 normal years + 97 leap years
Step 2: Total odd days = 497
Step 3: 497 ÷ 7 = remainder 0
Step 4: Therefore the day repeats.
